doc_summary: Hubinger proposes that major labs commit to monitoring for deceptive alignment and running experiments to predict it, laying out what evidence would convince us (behavior changing with oversight, internal evidence via interpretability) and a ladder of demonstrations plus precursor experiments. He stresses the difficulty of tricking one's own model and the risk of overfitting to easy-to-find or narrow definitions.

items.claim: Treats behavior that changes depending on whether oversight is present or absent as the clearest evidence of deception, so setups should vary perceived oversight while keeping real oversight tight enough to catch the behavior.
items.quote: The most straightforward way to produce evidence of a model’s deception is to find a situation where it changes what it’s doing based on the presence or absence of oversight.

items.claim: Recognises that honeypot-style tests require tricking the model into believing oversight is lax, which becomes harder as models get more capable, which is a core realism problem.
items.quote: we have to produce a situation where oversight appears to be lax, but is actually still tight enough that we do in fact catch the deception—that is, we have to trick our own model, which could be quite difficult for relatively advanced models.

items.claim: Prefers evidence of an ulterior motive that is internal or occurs in real or realistic situations over prompted or simulated behavior, because prompted results only test the model+prompt combination.
items.quote: this only tests for the deception or lack thereof of the given model + prompt combination—it doesn’t help us understand whether the model on its own is deceptive or whether it’s only deceptive when prompted in particular ways.

items.claim: Ranks demonstrations by how convincing and dangerous they are, with real-world misalignment emerging when checking ability drops at the top and simulated or prompted evidence lower.
items.quote: The model displays clear misalignment in a simulated environment that only occurs in situations where the ability of some overseer in the environment to check its behavior is more limited.

items.claim: Prefers testing for deceptive precursors (convergent instrumental goals like avoiding shutdown, non-myopia) over direct deception because direct tests are likely to be negative now while precursors share the same instrumental reasoning.
items.quote: When do models exhibit convergent instrumental goals? If, for example, trained to be helpful to humans, when do models exhibit a convergent desire to avoid shutdown?

items.claim: Distrusts testbeds that capture only the easiest-to-find examples fitting a current definition, insisting a lab demonstration must reflect the real issues to be useful.
items.quote: for an example of deceptive alignment in laboratory to actually be useful to study, it needs to actually be a good testbed that reflects the real issues.

items.claim: Warns against overfitting to the current conception of the failure mode and against treating a weak commitment or negative results as having solved the problem.
items.quote: we might end up ignoring an actually concerning failure mode simply because it doesn’t satisfy our current understanding of deceptive alignment—an understanding that could end up being quite far off from the failure modes that actually end up being problematic.

items.claim: Endorses running many experiments expected to be negative as the right safety posture, rather than only pursuing tests likely to produce positive results.
items.quote: running lots of negative experiments is what safety is supposed to look like: aggressively testing for failure modes even if you think they’re probably not present.

items.claim: In a setup, probe a model via conditional framings (e.g., offering a chance to come clean, or switching audience from outsiders to in-group) instead of only observing default behavior, because deceptive behavior may only surface when the model believes the audience or incentives changed.
items.quote: interview it in a situation where 4channers might try to pretend to normies that they don’t have awful beliefs, then move to a situation where the model is talking to a fellow 4channer and see if they come clean.

items.claim: Expects that deceptive models need not be explicitly planning deception in advance, so tests should present actual opportunities (e.g., seizing power) rather than rely on finding pre-existing plans.
items.quote: A model that has never seen a situation where there is an opportunity to seize power need not be carefully planning out what it would do in such a situation any more than a factory cleaning robot need be planning for what to do if it someday found itself in a jungle instead of a factory.

items.claim: Expects that the space of deceptive models includes ones that are easy to catch (short horizons, confused about simulation level, poor at hiding), so honeypots are worth running.
items.quote: are confused about what level of simulation they’re in such that they defect to break out of an inner simulation only to find themselves in an outer simulation,
